Let x be the number of ways to color the faces of the dodecahedron with $12$ different colors, where two colorings are identical if one can be rotated to obtain the other. Compute $\frac{x}{12!}$.\n<image1>

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Use Burnside's lemma for the rotational symmetry group acting on assignments of the 12 distinct colors to the 12 faces. There are 12! unrestricted assignments. The rotational symmetry group of a regular dodecahedron has 60 elements. The identity rotation fixes all 12! assignments. Any non-identity rotation moves at least one face to a different face; since all colors are distinct and used on different faces, such a moved face cannot retain the same coloring under the rotation. Therefore every non-identity rotation fixes 0 assignments. Burnside's lemma gives x = (12!)/60, so x/12! = 1/60.

method.method_draft: Use Burnside's lemma on the action of the rotational symmetry group of the regular dodecahedron on the set of all assignments of the 12 distinct colors to the 12 faces. There are 12! unrestricted colorings. The rotational symmetry group of a regular dodecahedron has 60 elements. Because all 12 colors are distinct, any non-identity rotation moves at least one face to a different face and therefore cannot fix any coloring. Thus Burnside gives x = (12! + 0 + ... + 0)/60 = 12!/60, so x/12! = 1/60.

method.method_draft: Count the size of each rotation-equivalence class directly by anchoring an orientation. For any colored dodecahedron with all faces differently colored, rotating it can place any one of its 12 colored faces into a chosen reference position, such as the front/top face. After that face is fixed, there are 5 possible rotations about the axis through that face, corresponding to the 5 edges/neighboring positions of the pentagon. Hence each coloring has exactly 12 · 5 = 60 rotated copies, and no two of these copies coincide because the colors are all distinct. Therefore the number of equivalence classes is x = 12!/60, so x/12! = 1/60.
